speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) whether the demand for Allied Health Professionals (AHPs) has increased between 2019 and 2023 and, if so, by how much; and (b) in each year from 2019 to 2023, what has the attrition rate of AHPs been in (i) public acute hospitals (ii) public community hospitals (iii) public long-term care facilities and (iv) polyclinics.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: asked the Minister for Health (a) how does the attrition rate of Allied Health Professionals (AHPs) in public acute hospitals, public community hospitals, public long-term care facilities and polyclinics compare with those of doctors and nurses; (b) what measures are being considered to address attrition rate of AHPs; and (c) whether such measures include an increase in remuneration.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Due to our growing healthcare needs, the demand for Allied Health Professionals (AHPs) have been growing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Ministry of Health (MOH) continues to work with our public healthcare clusters, community care organisations and our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) to train, attract and retain AHPs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There need to be good career prospects and opportunities for professional development, a conducive workplace environment and salaries will have to be competitive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In this regard, the public healthcare institutions (PHIs) had increased the starting salaries of AHPs in 2023.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Since 2021, MOH has also supported salary enhancements in the community care sector, including for AHPs.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Is the attrition rate of AHPs higher or lower than doctors and nurses?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I am not sure if the Senior Parliamentary Secretary answered my original question on that.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Are the retention and career progression needs of AHPs being, in any way, prioritised behind those of doctors and nurses, despite them playing a very critical role in the recovery of patients?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The Member is right in that they play a very critical role.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have been engaging AHPs in developing a strategy because they are part of the healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And, as you know, we are transforming our healthcare sector – there will be Age Well SG and Healthier SG – and it is important for them to also play that role in this endeavour to have a common understanding of the focus areas and transformation of the allied health delivery that needs to meet these national strategies.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We have been working with them to future-proof the allied health workforce to handle future challenges of the ageing population and improving population health and outcomes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: They are part of the ecosystem, and we are working together to help us work that journey of transforming the healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: What proportion of APHs in PHIs are foreigners and how does this compare to the proportion of nurses who are foreigners?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
text: And secondly, how is the Ministry encouraging more Singaporeans to take up careers as AHPs?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I do not have the data now on hand, as far as the numbers of foreign AHPs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In respect of the second question on how we are working to enhance the AHP profession, we have been doing this on a few fronts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We are working with the IHLs to increase local training pipelines with healthcare employers to attract and retain quality manpower.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In respect of the foreign AHPs, we also value them.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And if they demonstrate their commitment to Singapore, we are also prepared to grant them permanent resident (PR) status.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, that is one thing that is quite encouraging, I believe.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We also have healthcare career conversion programmes for mid-career locals to undergo relevant trainings through our IHLs for selected AHP professionals.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: These are some of the efforts that we have put in place to enhance the profession and to uplift the standing of the profession within the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I note that the Senior Parliamentary Secretary mentioned that the community care AHPs had experienced a decline in the attrition rate, as opposed to the overall slight increase in attrition rate for the other sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I am wondering whether the Ministry has given any consideration into what might account for this differential because understanding this might give us some insight into how to improve retention in the overall sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: AHPs are in the public healthcare sector as well as in the community care sector because they also support some of our roles in the public institutions.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, in terms of the decline, I think there are so many different factors, clearly, and we are looking at how we can improve this.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Part of it is salaries and the standing of some of these professions within the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think, over time, we have learnt, and we have also been engaging these professions to understand what are some of the challenges and the workplace issues they may be facing.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: And so, these are the things that will inform us as we have these discussions, moving forward, with the AHPs in enhancing the profession, in making them also part of the larger ecosystem, as we transform our healthcare sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: I acknowledge what the Senior Parliamentary Secretary mentioned about how salaries.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: As an economist, that is an intuitive explanation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But my understanding is that in the community care sector, if anything, salaries are slightly lower than compared to overall.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: So, I would truly urge the Ministry to look much more carefully into why attrition rates seem to be lower in the community care sector compared to overall.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Indeed, we have been working with the community care sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: You have heard announcements recently about Award for Nurses' Grace, Excellence and Loyalty (ANGEL) and we are also working with the community sector, to make sure that it is also something that can translate into that sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: So, this is something we will continue to review, look at and enhance when appropriate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I should start by declaring that I am a medical doctor practising at a PHI and I look after cancer patients as part of that journey.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Can I put it to MOH, is there a role to take a detailed look at the evolving landscape of skills across our AHPs, a skills-based assessment and analysis, to see how we can better retain and develop our AHPs?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We recognise today that in healthcare, for medical professionals and nursing professionals, deep skills are involved.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And it is likewise the case for AHPs, whether these are the therapists, occupational therapists or speech therapists.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, in the care of patients who have cancer running in multiple family members, there is a group of experts called genetic counsellors who provide very important support for the medical care team as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And so, if we look at the emerging role across all these AHPs as having deep skills, skills that can be deepened, best in class in Singapore and across the world, would MOH consider that as a way of refreshing or relooking at how we recognise AHPs as an important and key part of our healthcare system?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In response, I will just highlight a few things.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think, firstly, indeed, this is the direction that we are going in terms of enhancing skills and making sure that there are sufficient manpower and resources within each domain.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: As you know, the AHPs are a mixed bag; there are many different types of specialties.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: I have got one more question to the Senior Parliamentary Secretary.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: As part of this review which the Senior Parliamentary Secretary has mentioned, will MOH also look at best-in-class jurisdictions around the world and learn from the experience of how AHPs' career journeys, retention, skills and all these have been developed, in jurisdictions such as the United Kingdom (UK), in Europe or in the United States (US)?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: Will MOH consider looking at that as well as part of this overall landscape review?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I think that is a brilliant suggestion from my fellow Jurong Group Representation Constituency mate.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I note that the Ministry had published salary guidelines for the community care sector and the Senior Parliamentary Secretary talked about it just now.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would say I have received much positive feedback from healthcare professionals and their managers; in particular, from the larger private sector community care and age care groups, on this guidance.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They found it very useful in attracting and retaining staff.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, in my union and constituency work, I continue to receive wage and welfare grievances from employees of smaller clinics.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And salaries can be stagnated for years; sometimes, at levels lower than the Progressive Wage Model (PWM).

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I appreciate that private sector salaries are best left to market forces, for this group of workers, what more can MOH do to engage the owners of small health businesses and to ensure that our workers have dignified livelihoods?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: From our experience, the assessment or the complaint or feedback that we have gotten is there is a move from the public sector into the private healthcare sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Because of the competitive nature of the competitive salary, we take that into account as we think about whether to have a salary guideline for this space.
